Once the corrosion allowance is taken into account, the reboiler wall thickness comes to 35 mm, and it is the allowance, rather than the pressure loading on its own, that lifts it above the calculated minimum. The allowance is extra metal held against wastage over the design life, and both the shell course and the channel take it in full, because the solvent wets both faces and the wastage rates do not differ enough to justify two thicknesses. The wetting itself is set by the regeneration loop: solvent leaves the absorber loaded, gives up its load in the reboiler circuit, and the lean solvent pump returns it at the full rate, so neither face of the wall sees a milder duty than the other.

The gasket comparison is a much narrower question than the wall question. Two candidate materials remain in contention, and the comparison between them runs on temperature limit alone, because cost, availability and seating behaviour have already been settled elsewhere in the design and neither material fails on any of those grounds. The higher-rated material is preferred. Its limit stands further above the temperature that the joint reaches when a regeneration upset sends hotter solvent through the reboiler, and a gasket that is working close to its limit during such an excursion will tend to relax and weep long before the metal is at risk. $\Delta P$ across the reboiler does not separate the two materials; both seal at the working $\Delta P$ under the specified bolt load, and pressure containment is carried by the wall rather than by the joint.
